analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from dodging US taxes by moving their headquarters to tax-haven countries.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax corporate inversions as if they never left the US has 0 cosponsors and has sat untouched in the Ways and Means Committee since its February 11, 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, a US company can move its legal home to a low-tax country in an 'inversion' and, in many cases, pay less US tax while keeping its factories, offices, and customers in America. This bill rewrites Section 7874 of the tax code so that such a company is treated, for tax purposes, as if it were still a US corporation if its former US owners kept more than half the stock, or if its top managers stayed in the US and a quarter or more of its employees, payroll, assets, or income remain American. Companies with genuine, substantial business operations in the country they moved to are still exempt. The change reaches back to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, when the IRS first cracked down on inversions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary US taxpayers, who otherwise make up for revenue lost when profitable American companies legally relocate on paper to low-tax countries while keeping their operations here. Domestic competitors that never invert also benefit, because the tax advantage of flipping headquarters disappears.

how_it_helps.text: A foreign-reincorporated company is taxed as a US corporation if former American shareholders own more than 50% of it, instead of the current 60% surrogate threshold, or if its management and control remain primarily in the US alongside significant domestic business activity (at least 25% of employees, employee compensation, assets, or income).
The rules reach back to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, so companies that inverted in recent years could not keep the tax benefit of deals already completed.
Companies that truly moved substantial operations abroad are still exempt, so the bill targets paper relocations rather than genuine foreign expansion.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that have inverted or plan to — drug and medical-device makers are the classic cases — along with their shareholders, who would face higher US tax bills, and the law and accounting firms that earn fees structuring such deals.

drawbacks.text: The change applies retroactively to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, meaning companies that completed inversions years ago would face new taxes on old transactions — a fairness objection an honest supporter must acknowledge.

The new 'management and control' test depends on Treasury regulations to decide when executives count as US-based, adding complexity and dispute risk, and the substantial-foreign-activity exception starts from regulations issued January 18, 2017 that critics called lenient; the Treasury Secretary could tighten those thresholds but the bill does not tighten them itself.
Sweeping definitions could reach companies with real, growing foreign operations, even with the exemption, increasing compliance costs across multinationals, not just inversion specialists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — a company should not cut its US tax bill by swapping its legal address while keeping its business here — is straightforwardly aimed at a tax benefit ordinary taxpayers ultimately fund. The main design flaws are retroactivity and reliance on detailed regulations that could make compliance expensive and litigious; the lenient 2017-regulation baseline for the exemption also leaves room for well-advised companies to escape. On balance the bill helps taxpayers more than it hurts them, but it is a broad, retroactive change that would have faced serious transition disputes if it ever moved.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was filed, with zero cosponsors and no hearing or markup since — it has simply sat in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett (D-TX) introduced the bill on February 11, 2026, and it was referred that same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax legislation.
No other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

The bill would rewrite the corporate inversion rules (Section 7874) so a foreign-reincorporated company is treated as a US corporation if former US shareholders own more than 50% of it, or if its management and control remain primarily in the US with at least 25% of its employees, payroll, assets, or income in the country.

It applies to taxable years ending after May 8, 2014, with an exception for companies that have substantial real business activity in the country they moved to, measured against regulations issued January 18, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that have used or could use inversion structures are unaffected so far: because the bill has stalled without even cosponsors, no tax change has taken effect and the existing inversion rules remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to his committee; the only member supporting it.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as chair and has scheduled no hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes and no cosponsors to measure; the bill's support is one Democrat and it sits with a Republican-controlled committee that has taken no action.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations using or considering inversion structures (notably drug and medical-device makers)
industries.note: The bill would strip the tax advantage of relocating a legal headquarters abroad while keeping US operations, subjecting such companies to US tax on their worldwide income. Their gain under the status quo comes at the expense of the broader tax base that other taxpayers support.

industries.industry: Corporate tax planning advisers (major accounting and law firms)
industries.note: Fewer inversion transactions and related restructurings would mean less fee income from structuring and defending these deals. Their interest in keeping the current rules runs against the taxpayers who fund the revenue the rules preserve.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance: a sole-sponsored corporate tax increase with no cosponsors rarely gets a hearing, and the Ways and Means chair has shown none. The realistic best case is that its language is folded into a larger tax bill, which would require support nowhere visible in the record.
